feedback: If the prediction is a straight rising line ('you're still heating it, so it gets hotter'), plot the real curve with its plateau and explain the energy is spent rearranging particles during the change; read the flat region as the melting point.
Full understanding needs the reason — 'energy goes into the state change, not into heating' — not just reading the plateau.
For the washing-line puzzle: evaporation happens from the surface at any temperature, so water leaves slowly even in the cold; it does not require reaching 100°C.
For freezing: expect a flat part at the freezing point (0°C for water) as energy is removed and particles lock into the solid arrangement — the mirror image of melting.
activities.intendedInsight: The thermometer stays at about 0°C while ice and water coexist in a well-stirred mixture because the incoming energy overcomes the forces/arrangement holding the solid particles (changing state) rather than raising particle speed; only once all the ice has melted does the temperature rise clearly again. Evaporation from a surface occurs at any temperature, which is why cold wet clothes dry.
learnerActions: Before doing anything, predict the temperature-vs-time graph for a thermometer in crushed ice that is heated steadily — especially what happens while ice and water coexist — and write WHY you predict that shape.
Heat crushed ice (taken to start at 0°C) steadily, stirring gently, with a thermometer in it and record the temperature over time, plotting the trace.

Compare your prediction with your real trace, which should show an approximately flat region at or near 0°C while ice and water coexist (a well-stirred mixture stays close to 0°C; small rises can happen if water near the heat source warms before all the ice has melted).
Explain where the heat energy 'goes' during the flat part, and answer: would freezing water show a flat part too, and at what temperature and why?
Apply the idea to a puzzle: wet clothes dry on a cold washing line — how, if water only turns to gas at 100°C?
activities.title: Predict-Observe-Explain: heating crushed ice
